audit.binary_validation_scope: Original executable SHA256 retained as historical provenance; frozen runner checked it during execution. Analysis neither requires nor executes that binary. All nonbinary frozen source/evidence pins are verified.
audit.input_hash_scope: All recorded SHA256 formats/specs/seeds audited; arrays are not retained or independently regenerated by this analysis.

analysis_method.seed_derivation: First16 SHA256 bytes of seed:label as little-endian integer; NumPy PCG64
analysis_method.ci: Pointwise percentile 95% bootstrap of 30 trials, linear quantiles; no simultaneous correction
analysis_method.paired_models: Resample paired within-condition ratios across the 30 common-input trials
analysis_method.endpoints: Separate bootstrap samples for independently seeded first/last parameter trials
analysis_method.curve_error: Absolute relative mean error at all21points; normalized RMSE divides by mean reference curve
analysis_method.original_uncertainty: Original std retained as reported; no original SE, CI or trial count inferred

manuscript.title: [Re] Comparison-count benefits in learning-augmented priority queues
manuscript.abstract: Learning-augmented priority queues can reduce expensive true-key comparisons, but replicating that result requires precise advice, tie and counting conventions. We partially replicate the sorting experiments of Benomar and Coester with an independently authored C++ implementation checked against their released Python code. Across 11,340 runs, the class-quality and decay responses agree with the original findings; median pointwise relative errors are below 0.16% on every curve at the two main-paper sizes. Comparison benefits remain conditional on advice quality, with the uninformative class endpoint exceeding the analytic heap reference. A separate extension identifies historical node-map ownership: last-occurrence cleanup reduces drained-queue traced memory from 35.18 to 0.024 MiB, with the ownership effect repeated on a second host. Native graph controls favor a direct heap on all seven tested workloads on both hosts. The artifact separates replicated comparison-count evidence from these additional memory and runtime measurements and provides reproducible input generation, raw counts and verification procedures.

methods_blocks.text: The primary engine is separately authored C++17. Before execution, 666 small shared-input cases matched the pinned Python sorting functions exactly in cumulative clean and dirty counts and in complete comparator-call trace digests. The optimized and AddressSanitizer/UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer builds both passed. Four malformed-input controls failed closed, and six checks matched the released analytic heap expression.

Within each new condition, the three methods share the final rank-advice array, the geometric-height sequence by insertion step, and the insertion permutation where applicable. Offline sorting instead stably orders the ordinal keys by advice. Repetitions and parameter cells use independent, domain-separated advice, order and height streams. This pairing preserves each method's marginal experiment while differing from the original unseeded, interleaved algorithm loops.

The condition grid, source hashes, claim-specific analysis rules and published references were privately frozen before primary execution. This is a documented computational freeze, not an externally registered preregistration. The run executed on the Apple M1 MacBook Air under CPython 3.13.3 and NumPy 2.2.4, using Apple Clang 15 with C++17, -O3 and -DNDEBUG. Each model record constructs fresh queue state and checks the entire ordinal output. No sorting wall-time claim is made.

Pointwise intervals use 5,000 deterministic percentile-bootstrap resamples of our thirty runs. Paired model ratios resample shared conditions together; endpoint contrasts resample independently seeded endpoint cells separately. Intervals are pointwise, without simultaneous coverage correction. Every planned cell and recorded failure is retained, and no parameter or seed was retuned after observing the primary counts.

results_blocks.text: All 3,780 planned shared-input conditions and 11,340 model runs completed, with exact ordinal-output checks passing for every run. This yields 378 model/parameter means with 30 replicates each. The new records and all earlier graph timing records are kept separate.

The curves closely follow the published comparison-count behavior. Across the twelve curves at the two main-paper sizes, median pointwise absolute relative errors range from 0.028% to 0.151%; the largest individual relative error is 0.743%. For the six 1,000-key released-aggregate curves, the largest individual error is 4.650%. Table 1 reports every curve, including the smaller-size deviations.

results_blocks.caption: Table 1. Agreement of replicated means with the available references. At n = 1,000, reference values are released aggregate means; at larger sizes they are vector-derived plotted means from the final paper. Relative errors use the reference mean as denominator. Normalized RMSE is whole-curve RMSE divided by the arithmetic mean of its 21 reference means. These are descriptive agreement measures.

results_blocks.text: Figures 1 and 2 overlay the independently generated means and the published references at the main-paper sizes. Solid lines with open markers show this replication; dashed lines show the published means. The narrow shaded bands are pointwise 95% bootstrap intervals from our 30 replicates. No original standard errors or distributional-equivalence claim are inferred from these overlays.

results_blocks.caption: Figure 1. Partial replication of the original Figure 2: clean comparisons per key under class predictions. Both ordinate axes are logarithmic. The plotted class parameter zero is implemented as one class. Published and replicated curves largely overlap at this scale. The dotted horizontal line is the released analytic binary-heap reference, not a timed heap.

Figure 2. Partial replication of the original Figure 3: clean comparisons per key under decay predictions. The horizontal coordinate divides the timestep parameter by floor(n sqrt(n)); this rescales the original main-paper axis without changing the experiments. Better advice is at the left. Published and replicated curves largely overlap at this scale. The dotted line is the analytic binary-heap reference.

results_blocks.text: All eighteen endpoint contrasts have the expected direction: increasing the class parameter from its first to last value reduces the mean clean count, while increasing decay from zero to its maximum increases it, for all three methods and all three sizes. Each pointwise 95% bootstrap interval for the endpoint difference excludes zero in that direction.

results_blocks.caption: Table 2. Replicated mean clean comparisons per key at the first and last parameter values. Class start/end correspond to plotted c = 0/n; decay start/end correspond to t = 0/floor(n sqrt(n)). The full pointwise and endpoint interval tables are in the artifact.

results_blocks.text: The advantage over the analytic heap reference depends on advice quality. Pointwise bootstrap intervals lie below that reference in 369 of 378 cells. The nine remaining cells are the lowest-quality class endpoint, across all three sizes and methods; their intervals lie above it. All twenty other sampled class levels and all sampled decay levels lie below the reference. Thus the replication supports substantial comparison-count benefits over the tested useful-advice range while preserving the unfavorable uninformative-class endpoint visible in the original curves.

The relative ordering of prediction interfaces is also preserved: at the highest class parameter and at zero decay, offline advice requires about one clean comparison per key, and online and dirty/clean advice require about two. Model-to-model paired ratios and every observed heap-crossing bracket are reported in the artifact. The original qualitative description of comparable performance is not converted into an arbitrary numerical equivalence margin.

Original per-run observations and random states are not provided in the pinned artifact. The paper states a nominal thirty runs per plotted point, while the saved 1,000-key aggregates do not document their effective trial count. The published n = 100,000 class heap line corresponds to approximately 17.557000 comparisons per key; the released analytic expression gives 17.557310. We retain that small plot/reference discrepancy and calibrate the vector-derived means using the printed axis ticks, rather than adjusting a scale to force agreement.

manuscript.conclusion: Within the declared sorting subset, the comparison-count benefits replicate closely across both prediction-error models, three queue interfaces and three input sizes. The full curves preserve both useful-advice gains and the unfavorable uninformative-class endpoint. The independent implementation, explicit counting convention and published-reference extraction make that assessment reproducible. The separate ownership and native-runtime studies extend the artifact evaluation under different workloads and advice interfaces; they do not replace the original comparison metric or invalidate its theoretical cost model. For maintainers, the ownership fix is to delete a key's sl.nodes entry when its last live occurrence is extracted; node links can be left intact. The replication and extension together make both the published comparison result and practical implementation costs reproducible.
